source_text: ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΟΜΙΛΙΑ ΠΡΟΣ ΤΟΥΣ ΠΛΟΥΤΟΥΝΤΑΣ –Εἴρηται καὶ πρώην ἡμῖν τὰ περὶ τοῦ νεανίσκου τούτου, καὶ μέμνηται πάντως ὅ γε φιλόπονος ἀκροατὴς τῶν ἐξητασμένων τότε· πρῶτον μὲν, ὅτι οὐχ ὁ αὐτός ἐστι τῷ παρὰ τῷ Λουκᾷ νομικῷ. Ὁ μὲν γὰρ πειρασ τὴς ἦν, εἰρωνικὰς τὰς ἐρωτήσεις ποιούμενος· οὗτος δὲ, ὑγιῶς μὲν ἐρω τῶν, οὐκ εὐπειθῶς δὲ παραδεχόμενος. Οὐ γὰρ ἂν ἀπῆλθεν ἐπὶ ταῖς τοιαύ ταις ἀποκρίσεσιν τοῦ Κυρίου λυπούμενος, εἰ καταφρονητικῶς αὐτῷ προσῆγε τὰς πεύσεις. Διόπερ οἱονεὶ μικτὸν αὐτοῦ τὸ ἦθος ἡμῖν ἀνεφαίνετο· πῆ μὲν ἐπαινετὸν δεικνύοντος τοῦ λόγου, πῆ δὲ ἀθλιώτατον καὶ πάντη ἀπεγνωσμέ νον. Τὸ μὲν γὰρ γνωρίσαι τὸν ἀληθῶς διδάσκαλον, καὶ παρελθόντα τὴν Φαρισαίων ἀλαζονείαν, καὶ νομικῶν οἴησιν, καὶ γραμματέων ὄχλον, τὴν προσηγορίαν ταύτην ἀναθεῖναι τῷ μόνῳ ἀληθινῷ καὶ ἀγαθῷ διδασκάλῳ, τοῦτο ἦν ὃ ἐπῃνεῖτο. Καὶ μέντοι τὸ φανῆναι φροντίδος ἄξιον ποιούμενον πῶς ἂν τῆς αἰωνίου κληρονομήσειε ζωῆς, ἀποδεκτὸν καὶ τοῦτο. Ἐκεῖνο δὲ λοιπὸν ἐλέγχει αὐτοῦ τὴν ὅλην προαίρεσιν, οὐ πρὸς τὸ ἀληθινῶς καλὸν ἀποβλέπουσαν, ἀλλὰ τὸ τοῖς πολλοῖς ἀρέσκον περισκοποῦσαν· τὸ, μαθόντα παρὰ τοῦ ἀληθινοῦ διδασκάλου μαθήματα σωτήρια, μὴ ἐγγράψαι τῇ ἑαυτοῦ καρδίᾳ, μηδὲ εἰς ἔργον ἀγαγεῖν τὰ διδάγματα, ἀλλ' ἀπελθεῖν ἀθυμοῦντα, τῷ πάθει τῆς φιλοπλουτίας ἐσκοτωμένον. Τοῦτο δὲ τὴν ἀνωμαλίαν τῶν τρόπων, καὶ τὸ πρὸς ἑαυτὸν ἀσύμφωνον ἀπελέγχει. Διδάσκαλον λέγεις, καὶ τὰ μαθητῶν οὐ ποιεῖς; Ἀγαθὸν ὁμολογεῖς, καὶ τὰ διδόμενα παραπέμπῃ; Καίτοι ὅ γε ἀγαθὸς ἀγαθῶν ἐστι παρεκτικὸς δηλονότι. Καὶ ἐρωτᾷς μὲν περὶ τῆς αἰωνίου ζωῆς· ἐλέγχῃ δὲ ὅλως τῇ ἀπολαύσει τοῦ παρόντος βίου προσδεδεμένος. Τί δέ σοι χαλεπὸν, ἢ βαρὺ, ἢ ὑπέρογκον ῥῆμα ὁ διδάσκαλος προετείνατο; Πώλησόν σου τὰ ὑπάρχοντα, καὶ δὸς πτωχοῖς· Εἴ σοι προέβαλε πόνους γεωργικοὺς, ἢ τοὺς ἐξ ἐμπορίας κινδύνους, ἢ ὅσα ἄλλα τοῖς χρηματιζομένοις ἐπίπονα πρόσεστιν, ἔδει σε λυπηθῆναι δυσφο ροῦντα τῷ ἐπιτάγματι· εἰ δὲ οὕτως διὰ ῥᾳδίας ὁδοῦ, οὐδένα πόνον ἐχού σης οὐδὲ ἱδρῶτα, ἐπαγγέλλεταί σε κληρονόμον τῆς αἰωνίου ζωῆς ἀπο δείξειν, οὐ χαίρεις τῇ εὐκολίᾳ τῆς σωτηρίας, ἀλλ' ἀπέρχῃ ὀδυνώμενος τὴν ψυχὴν καὶ πενθῶν, καὶ ποιεῖς σεαυτῷ ἄχρηστα πάντα ὅσα σοι προπεπόνηται. Εἰ γὰρ οὐκ ἐφόνευσας, ὡς σὺ φῂς, οὔτε ἐμοίχευσας, οὔτε ἔκλεψας, οὔτε κατεμαρτύρησάς τινος μαρτυρίαν ψευδῆ, ἀνόνητον σεαυτῷ ποιεῖς τὴν περὶ ταῦτα σπουδὴν, μὴ προστιθεὶς τὸ λεῖπον, δι' οὗ μόνου δυνήσῃ εἰσελθεῖν εἰς τὴν βασιλείαν τοῦ Θεοῦ. Καὶ εἰ μὲν ἰατρὸς ἐπηγγέλλετο κολοβώματα μελῶν ἐκ φύσεως ἢ ἐξ ἀῤῥωστίας προσόντα σοι διορθώσασθαι, οὐκ ἂν ἠθύμεις ἀκούων· ἐπειδὴ δὲ ὁ μέγας τῶν ψυχῶν ἰατρὸς τέλειόν σε ποιῆσαι βούλεται τοῖς καιριωτάτοις ἐλλείποντα, οὐ δέχῃ τὴν χάριν, ἀλλὰ πενθεῖς καὶ σκυθρωπάζεις. Ἐκείνης μὲν γὰρ δῆλος εἶ τῆς ἐντολῆς μακρὰν ὑπάρχων, καὶ ψευδῶς σεαυτῷ προσμαρτυρήσας αὐτὴν, ὅτι ἠγάπησας τὸν πλησίον σου ὡς σεαυτόν. Ἰδοὺ γὰρ τὸ παρὰ τοῦ Κυρίου προταθὲν ἐλέγχει σε παμπληθὲς τῆς ἀληθινῆς ἀγάπης ἀπολειπόμενον. Εἰ γὰρ ὅπερ διεβεβαιώσω ἀληθὲς ἦν, ὅτι ἐφύλαξας ἐκ νεότητος τὴν ἐντολὴν τῆς ἀγάπης, καὶ τοσοῦτον ἀπέδωκας ἑκάστῳ ὅσον καὶ σεαυτῷ, πόθεν σοι ἡ τῶν χρημάτων αὕτη περιουσία; Δαπανητικὸν γὰρ πλούτου ἡ θεραπεία τῶν δεομένων· ὀλίγα μὲν ἑκάστου πρὸς τὴν ἀναγκαίαν ἐπιμέλειαν δεχομένου, πάντων δὲ ὁμοῦ καταμεριζομένων τὰ ὄντα, καὶ περὶ ἑαυτοὺς δαπανώντων. Ὥστε ὁ ἀγαπῶν τὸν πλησίον ὡς ἑαυτὸν οὐδὲν περισσότερον κέκτηται τοῦ πλησίον· ἀλλὰ μὴν φαίνῃ ἔχων κτήματα πολλά. Πόθεν ταῦτα; ἢ δῆλον ὅτι τὴν οἰκείαν ἀπόλαυσιν προτιμοτέραν τῆς τῶν πολλῶν παραμυθίας ποιούμενος. Ὅσον οὖν πλεονάζεις τῷ πλούτῳ, τοσοῦτον ἐλλείπεις τῇ ἀγάπῃ. Ἐπεὶ πάλαι ἂν ἐμελέτησας τῶν χρημάτων τὴν ἀλλοτρίωσιν, εἰ ἠγαπήκεις σου τὸν πλησίον. Νυνὶ δὲ προσπέφυκέ σοι τὰ χρήματα πλέον ἢ τὰ μέλη τοῦ σώματος, καὶ λυπεῖ σε αὐτῶν ὁ χωρισμὸς ὡς ἀκρωτηριασμὸς τῶν καιρίων. Εἰ γὰρ ἠμφίασας γυμ νὸν, εἰ ἔδωκας πεινῶντι τὸν ἄρτον σου, εἰ ἡ θύρα σου ἠνέῳκτο παντὶ ξένῳ, εἰ ἐγένου πατὴρ ὀρφανῶν, εἰ παντὶ συνέπασχες ἀδυνάτῳ, ὑπὲρ ποίων ἂν ἐλυπήθης χρημάτων; Ποῦ δ' ἂν καὶ ἐδυσχέρανας ἀποτιθέμενος τὰ λειπόμενα, πάλαι μελετήσας αὐτὰ διανέμειν τοῖς ἐνδεέσιν; Εἶτα, ἐν μὲν πανηγύρει οὐδεὶς λυπεῖται προϊέμενος τὰ παρόντα καὶ ἀντικτώμενος τὰ ἐνδέοντα· ἀλλ' ὅσῳπερ ἂν ἐλάττονος τιμῆς τὰ πολυτίμητα πρίηται, τοσούτῳ χαίρει, ὡς λαμπροῦ αὐτῷ τοῦ συναλλάγματος γενομένου· σὺ δὲ λυπῇ, χρυσίον, καὶ ἀργύριον, καὶ κτήματα διδούς· τουτέστι, λίθους καὶ χοῦν παρεχόμενος, ἵνα κτήσῃ τὴν μακαρίαν ζωήν.
thought_title: The rich young man's mixed character and his failure of love
orientation: Basil opens his homily by recalling his previous discussion of the rich young man, distinguishing him from the lawyer in Luke and analyzing his mixed character before turning to the command to sell possessions.
pass_a_gloss: It has been said also previously by us the things about this young man, and the diligent hearer certainly remembers the things examined then: first, that he is not the same as the lawyer in Luke. For that one was a tempter, making ironic questions; but this one, asking soundly, but not accepting obediently. For he would not have gone away grieving at such answers of the Lord, if he had brought the questions to him contemptuously. Therefore his character appeared to us as it were mixed; in one way the account showing it praiseworthy, in another way most wretched and utterly despaired of. For the recognizing of the true teacher, and passing by the arrogance of the Pharisees, and the conceit of the lawyers, and the crowd of the scribes, the assigning of this title to the only true and good teacher, this was what was praised. And indeed the appearing to make worthy of care how he might inherit eternal life, this too was acceptable. But that remaining thing refutes his whole purpose, not looking toward the truly beautiful, but examining around what pleases the many: the having learned from the true teacher saving lessons, not writing them on his own heart, nor bringing the teachings to deed, but going away disheartened, darkened by the passion of love of wealth. And this refutes the unevenness of his ways, and the discordance with himself. You call him Teacher, and you do not do the things of disciples? You confess him good, and you pass by the things given? And yet the good one is clearly a provider of good things. And you ask about eternal life; but you are convicted of being wholly bound to the enjoyment of the present life. What difficult, or heavy, or excessive word did the teacher put before you? Sell your possessions, and give to the poor. If he had put before you agricultural labors, or the dangers from trade, or however many other painful things attend those who do business, you would have needed to grieve, distressed at the command; but if through so easy a road, having no labor nor sweat, he promises to show you an heir of eternal life, you do not rejoice at the ease of salvation, but you go away pained in soul and mourning, and you make useless for yourself all the things you labored at beforehand. For if you did not murder, as you say, nor commit adultery, nor steal, nor bear false witness against anyone, you make your zeal about these things unprofitable for yourself, not adding what is lacking, through which alone you will be able to enter into the kingdom of God. And if a physician promised to correct mutilations of limbs present to you from nature or from illness, you would not be disheartened hearing it; but since the great physician of souls wishes to make you complete, lacking in the most critical things, you do not receive the grace, but you mourn and are gloomy. For you are clearly far from that commandment, and you falsely bore witness to yourself about it, that you loved your neighbor as yourself. For behold, the thing put forward by the Lord convicts you of falling short of true love by a great deal. For if what you asserted was true, that you kept from youth the commandment of love, and you gave back to each as much as to yourself, whence to you this surplus of possessions? For the care of those in need is costly to wealth; each one receiving little for the necessary care, but all together dividing up the possessions, and spending them on themselves. So the one who loves his neighbor as himself possesses nothing more than his neighbor; but indeed you appear having many possessions. Whence these? Or is it clear that you make your own enjoyment more preferred than the comfort of the many? As much therefore as you abound in wealth, so much you fall short in love. Since long ago you would have practiced the alienation of possessions, if you had loved your neighbor. But now the possessions have grown onto you more than the limbs of the body, and their separation pains you like amputation of the vital parts. For if you had clothed the naked, if you had given your bread to the hungry, if your door had been opened to every stranger, if you had become father of orphans, if you had suffered with every powerless one, over what possessions would you have grieved? And where would you have been vexed, putting away the things left over, having long ago practiced distributing them to those in need? Then, in a festival no one grieves giving up the things present and acquiring the things lacking; but by however much he buys the very valuable things at a lesser price, by so much he rejoices, as a splendid bargain having happened to him; but you grieve, giving gold, and silver, and possessions; that is, providing stones and dust, in order that you may acquire the blessed life.

choices.why: The verb means to let pass, neglect, or dismiss; in context Basil contrasts confessing Christ as good with ignoring what he gives.
The perfect tense indicates prior effort; in context it refers to the commandments the young man claims to have kept, not general labor.
The articular participle is a substantive meaning the deficient thing; Basil refers to the one missing requirement, not a numbered item.
rejected: the one thing that is lacking

choices.why: καίριος means decisive, critical, opportune; it refers to what is most essential at the decisive moment, not physical vitality.
The compound with προσ- and the reflexive dative σεαυτῷ means to claim or attest something for oneself; the dative marks the beneficiary, not the object.

choices.term: Δαπανητικὸν γὰρ πλούτου ἡ θεραπεία τῶν δεομένων
choices.english: For the care of those in need is costly to wealth
choices.why: δαπανητικόν is an adjective taking a genitive of the thing affected; it describes care for the needy as expensive for wealth, not as an action consuming wealth.
rejected: Caring for those in need consumes wealth
The service of the needy spends wealth

pass_b_english: We spoke before about this young man, and the diligent hearer certainly remembers what we examined then. First, he is not the same as the lawyer in Luke. That man was a tester, asking questions ironically; this one asks soundly but does not receive the answers obediently. For he would not have gone away grieving at such answers from the Lord if he had brought his questions contemptuously. So his character appeared to us as mixed: the account showed him partly praiseworthy, partly most wretched and utterly despaired of. For recognizing the true teacher, passing by the arrogance of the Pharisees, the conceit of the lawyers, and the crowd of scribes, and giving this title to the only true and good teacher—this was what was praised. And indeed, appearing to make it a matter of concern how he might inherit eternal life—this too was acceptable. But the rest convicts his whole purpose, which did not look toward what is truly good but seeking what pleases the crowd: having learned saving lessons from the true teacher, he did not write them on his own heart, nor bring the teachings to deed, but went away disheartened, darkened by the passion of love of wealth. This convicts the unevenness of his ways and his discord with himself. You call him Teacher, and you do not do what students do? You confess him good, and you pass by what he gives? Yet surely the good one is a provider of good things. And you ask about eternal life, but you are convicted of being wholly bound to the enjoyment of the present life. What harsh, heavy, or excessive word did the teacher set before you? Sell your possessions and give to the poor (Matthew 19:21). If he had set before you agricultural labors, or the dangers of trade, or all the other toils that come to those who make money, you would have had reason to grieve, distressed at the command. But if by so easy a road, holding no labor or sweat, he promises to make you an heir of eternal life, do you not rejoice at the ease of salvation, but go away pained in soul and mourning, and make useless for yourself everything you labored at beforehand? For if you did not murder, as you say, nor commit adultery, nor steal, nor bear false witness against anyone, you make your zeal about these things unprofitable for yourself by not adding what is lacking, through which alone you will be able to enter the kingdom of God. If a physician promised to correct the mutilations of limbs that were yours by nature or from illness, you would not be disheartened to hear it. But when the great physician of souls wishes to make you complete, though you are lacking in the most critical things, you do not receive the grace, but mourn and are gloomy. For you are clearly far from that commandment, and you bore witness to yourself falsely, that you loved your neighbor as yourself (Matthew 19:19). For see, what the Lord set before you convicts you of falling far short of true love. For if what you asserted were true, that from youth you kept the commandment of love (Matthew 19:20), and you gave back to each as much as to yourself, where did this surplus of possessions come from? For the care of those in need is costly to wealth: each one receives little for his necessary care, but all together divide up what exists and spend it on themselves. So the one who loves his neighbor as himself possesses nothing more than his neighbor. But you clearly have many possessions. Where did these come from? It is clear that you make your own enjoyment more important than the relief of the many. So as much as you abound in wealth, so much you fall short in love. For long ago you would have practiced the giving away of your possessions, if you had loved your neighbor. But now possessions cling to you more than the limbs of your body, and separation from them grieves you like the amputation of your vital parts. For if you had clothed the naked, if you had given your bread to the hungry, if your door had been open to every stranger, if you had become a father to orphans, if you had suffered with every powerless person, over what possessions would you have grieved? Where would you have been distressed at putting away what remained, having long practiced distributing them to those in need? Then, at a festival no one grieves at giving up what he has and acquiring what he lacks; but the cheaper he buys what is costly, the more he rejoices, as though the exchange had turned out brilliantly for him. But you grieve at giving gold and silver and possessions—that is, at providing stones and dust—in order to acquire the blessed life.

problems.why: παραμυθία here means consolation/relief of the poor, not 'comfort' in a soft sense; 'relief' or 'consolation' better captures aid to those in need.

fixed: Changed 'the comfort of the many' to 'the relief of the many' because παραμυθία here means consolation/relief of the poor, not soft comfort.

problems.quote: examined around for what pleases the many
problems.why: περισκοποῦσαν means 'looking around for/seeking,' not 'examining around'; 'pleases the many' obscures that τοῖς πολλοῖς means 'the masses/common people,' not just 'many.'
ἀλλοτρίωσις means 'alienation/making over to another,' i.e., giving away, not 'estrangement' in the emotional sense; this is about dispossession, not alienation.
problems.fix: the giving away of your possessions

fixed: περισκοποῦσαν means 'looking around for/seeking,' not 'examining around'; τοῖς πολλοῖς means 'the crowd/masses,' so 'seeking what pleases the crowd' is correct.
ἀλλοτρίωσις means 'alienation/making over to another,' i.e., giving away, not 'estrangement' in the emotional sense; 'the giving away of your possessions' is correct.

dismissed.quote: You call him Teacher, and you do not do what students do? You confess him good, and you pass by what he gives?
dismissed.why: Basil addresses the rich young man in second person, but English shifts to third person 'him', confusing speaker.
dismissed.note: The English keeps the second person ('You call'); 'him' is Christ, the object of λέγεις, and the proposed fix is the same as the current text.
